newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda genocide tribunal adjourns.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda genocide tribunal adjourns.

text.p: The problem-plagued tribunal on Rwanda's 1994 genocide adjourned after a brief start on Thursday when the prosecution failed to present witnesses because they had not arrived from Rwanda, the court heard.
Rwanda swiftly blamed the U.N.-created tribunal for the snag, saying it applied for travel documents for the witnesses only two days ago.

"The tribunal is going to postpone until tomorrow (Friday) afternoon so that the prosecution can be allowed to present evidence," Laity Kama of Senegal, chairman of the three-person panel of judges, told the court.
Tribunal officials told reporters 31 witnesses, due to testify against Hutu former government official Jean-Paul Akayesu, had encountered visa problems.
Akayesu, 43, is charged with genocide and crimes against humanity during the four-month slaughter.

He is a former mayor in central Rwanda's Taba commune and has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The prosecution says the crimes were committed between April and June 1994 when an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.
"The witnesses are not here. They will arrive tomorrow afternoon because there is a problem with their visas," lead prosecutor Yacob Haile Mariam told reporters.
Rwanda's deputy Justice Minister Gerard Gahima told Reuters in a telephone interview his government was working hard to process passport applications for the witnesses.
Earlier during opening Thursday's session, Yacob outlined Akayesu's participation in the genocide.

"Akayesu lured 15 children to their deaths at a road block in Taba by saying their fathers were waiting for them but when they arrived a waiting crowd split their tender skulls with machetes," Yacob told the court.
He added: "Akayesu also ordered seriously wounded Tutsis to be thrown into the river where they drowned and watched Tutsis being chopped up with machetes and blunt tools."

Yacob detailed numerous witnesses he said would come to court to testify against Akayesu, ranging from a 69-year old Hutu woman beaten and tortured by Akayesu for hiding a Tutsi, to a western professor with three decades experience of Rwandan society.

The prosecutor said a young girl would tell how her brother was beaten and hacked to death on Akayesu's orders and another man, a political rival of Akayesu, would explain how Akayesu tried to hunt him down and have him killed.
Akayesu faces life imprisonment, the tribunal's maximum penalty, if convicted.

The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) tribunal, created by the U.N. Security Council in November 1994, has made a series of false starts with trials immediately being adjourned for procedural reasons.
U.N. headquarters in New York sent investigators and auditors to probe the tribunal and its prosecution office in Rwanda late last year. The inquiry's findings are unknown.

The Rwandan government is privately dismissive of the ICTR as an inept and wasteful exercise and has embarked on its own prosecutions against 90,000 detained Hutu suspects. The first two have been sentenced to death.
"The strategy of the defence will be to verify the credibility or the absence of credibility of prosecution witnesses," Nicolas Taingaye, one of Akayesu's three lawyers, told reporters.
In a rare boost for the tribunal, officials said a deal had been signed with Cameroon for the transfer of four leading genocide suspects held there.

Tribunal spokeswoman Beatrice Lacoste told reporters before Akayesu's trial opened that Theoneste Bagosora, a former senior army official, and three others would be flown from custody in Cameroon to the tribunal's jail in Tanzania.

Twenty-one people have been indicted by the tribunal including Akayesu. Eight suspects are still at large, seven are held in Arusha including Akayesu, four are in detention in Cameroon and the United States and Switzerland hold one each.
